claim: The persistence of experience-dependent changes in brain connectivity requires RNA localization and protein synthesis.
source: The persistence of experience-dependent changes in brain connectivity requires RNA localization and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about synaptic plasticity.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated a role for local translation in altering the structure and function of synapses during synapse formation and experience-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated a role for local translation in altering the structure and function of synapses during synapse formation and experience-dependent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings, as indicated by 'Previous studies'.

claim: RNAs were delivered throughout the arbor of the sensory neuron during synapse formation and synaptic plasticity.
source: Imaging of RNA localization and translation in cultured Aplysia sensory-motor neurons revealed that RNAs were delivered throughout the arbor of the sensory neuron, but that translation was enriched only at sites of synaptic contact and/or synaptic stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging experiments described in the manuscript, including FISH and live imaging data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Translation was enriched only at sites of synaptic contact and/or synaptic stimulation.
source: Imaging of RNA localization and translation in cultured Aplysia sensory-motor neurons revealed that RNAs were delivered throughout the arbor of the sensory neuron, but that translation was enriched only at sites of synaptic contact and/or synaptic stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including immunocytochemistry, translational reporters, and ribopuromycylation shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Calcium-dependent retrograde netrin-1/DCC receptor signaling plays a role in triggering local translation.
source: Investigation of the mechanisms that trigger local translation revealed a role for calcium-dependent retrograde netrin-1/DCC receptor signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with anti-DCC antibodies, netrin-1 application, and BAPTA calcium chelation shown in Figures 7-10.

claim: Spatially restricting gene expression by regulating local translation rather than by directing the delivery of mRNAs from nucleus to stimulated synapses maximizes the readiness of the entire neuronal arbor to respond to local cues.
source: Spatially restricting gene expression by regulating local translation rather than by directing the delivery of mRNAs from nucleus to stimulated synapses maximizes the readiness of the entire neuronal arbor to respond to local cues.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings showing equal RNA distribution but localized translation.

claim: Synapse formation and long-lasting experience-dependent synaptic plasticity require new RNA and protein synthesis.
source: Synapse formation and long-lasting experience-dependent synaptic plasticity require new RNA and protein synthesis (Kandel, 2001; Kalinovsky and Scheiffele, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons are dramatically polarized and compartmentalized cells, elaborating axonal and dendritic processes that extend long distances and forming thousands of synaptic connections with other neurons.
source: Neurons are dramatically polarized and compartmentalized cells, elaborating axonal and dendritic processes that extend long distances and forming thousands of synaptic connections with other neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established neurobiological knowledge.

claim: mRNAs that constitutively localize to axonal growth cones in immature neurons and to dendrites in mature neurons undergo stimulus-induced translation.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that mRNAs that constitutively localize to axonal growth cones in immature neurons and to dendrites in mature neurons undergo stimulus-induced translation, demonstrating that regulated translation of localized mRNAs provides one mechanism of spatially restricting neuronal gene expression (Aakalu et al., 2001; Job and Eberwine, 2001; Leung et al., 2006; Lyles et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2005; Tsokas et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Regulated translation of localized mRNAs provides one mechanism of spatially restricting neuronal gene expression.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that mRNAs that constitutively localize to axonal growth cones in immature neurons and to dendrites in mature neurons undergo stimulus-induced translation, demonstrating that regulated translation of localized mRNAs provides one mechanism of spatially restricting neuronal gene expression (Aakalu et al., 2001; Job and Eberwine, 2001; Leung et al., 2006; Lyles et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2005; Tsokas et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: Transcriptional inhibitors block late-phase LTP of rodent hippocampal synapses.
source: For example, transcriptional inhibitors block late-phase LTP of rodent hippocampal synapses (Frey et al., 1996; Nguyen et al., 1994) and long-term facilitation (LTF) of Aplysia sensory-motor synapses (Montarolo et al., 1986), indicating that translation of pre-existing localized mRNAs is not sufficient for late-LTP in hippocampus or for the persistence of LTF in Aplysia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Transcriptional inhibitors block long-term facilitation (LTF) of Aplysia sensory-motor synapses.
source: For example, transcriptional inhibitors block late-phase LTP of rodent hippocampal synapses (Frey et al., 1996; Nguyen et al., 1994) and long-term facilitation (LTF) of Aplysia sensory-motor synapses (Montarolo et al., 1986), indicating that translation of pre-existing localized mRNAs is not sufficient for late-LTP in hippocampus or for the persistence of LTF in Aplysia.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Translation of pre-existing localized mRNAs is not sufficient for late-LTP in hippocampus or for the persistence of LTF in Aplysia.
source: For example, transcriptional inhibitors block late-phase LTP of rodent hippocampal synapses (Frey et al., 1996; Nguyen et al., 1994) and long-term facilitation (LTF) of Aplysia sensory-motor synapses (Montarolo et al., 1986), indicating that translation of pre-existing localized mRNAs is not sufficient for late-LTP in hippocampus or for the persistence of LTF in Aplysia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental findings.

claim: Isolated Aplysia sensory neurites, severed from their somata and paired with motor neurons, undergo a form of serotonin (5HT)-induced LTF that does not last as long as the LTF in cultures containing intact SNs.
source: Similarly, when isolated Aplysia sensory neurites, severed from their somata, are paired with motor neurons, they undergo a form of serotonin (5HT)-induced LTF that does not last as long as the LTF in cultures containing intact SNs (Grabham et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Newly transcribed mRNAs are required for persistent synaptic plasticity.
source: Together these studies demonstrate that newly transcribed mRNAs are required for persistent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies on transcriptional inhibitors and isolated neurites.

claim: Depolarization increases the dendritic localization of beta-actin mRNA.
source: For example, depolarization has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of several mRNAs, including those encoding beta-actin (Tiruchinapalli et al., 2003), BDNF, and TrkB (Tongiorgi et al., 1997), while incubation with DHPG has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of the AMPA glutamate receptor GluA2 (Grooms et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Depolarization increases the dendritic localization of BDNF and TrkB mRNAs.
source: For example, depolarization has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of several mRNAs, including those encoding beta-actin (Tiruchinapalli et al., 2003), BDNF, and TrkB (Tongiorgi et al., 1997), while incubation with DHPG has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of the AMPA glutamate receptor GluA2 (Grooms et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Incubation with DHPG increases the dendritic localization of the AMPA glutamate receptor GluA2 mRNA.
source: For example, depolarization has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of several mRNAs, including those encoding beta-actin (Tiruchinapalli et al., 2003), BDNF, and TrkB (Tongiorgi et al., 1997), while incubation with DHPG has been shown to increase the dendritic localization of the AMPA glutamate receptor GluA2 (Grooms et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Neurotrophins regulate the concentration of specific mRNAs in axons of regenerating adult sensory neurons.
source: Similarly, neurotrophins have been reported to regulate the concentration of specific mRNAs in axons of regenerating adult sensory neurons (Willis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Neuronal activity induces transcription of genes whose transcripts are subsequently transported into dendrites, including the immediate early gene Arc.
source: Neuronal activity also induces transcription of genes whose transcripts are subsequently transported into dendrites, including for example the immediate early gene Arc (Link et al., 1995; Lyford et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The bclw transcript localizes to peripheral but not central axons of DRG neurons.
source: In situ hybridization images of the bclw transcript in a recent study from Cosker et al (2013) indicated that the mRNA localized to peripheral but not central axons of DRG neurons, suggesting that neurons are capable of directing transcripts from the soma to subsets of processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Neurons are capable of directing transcripts from the soma to subsets of processes.
source: In situ hybridization images of the bclw transcript in a recent study from Cosker et al (2013) indicated that the mRNA localized to peripheral but not central axons of DRG neurons, suggesting that neurons are capable of directing transcripts from the soma to subsets of processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited study on bclw transcript localization.

claim: A bifurcated Aplysia sensory neuron forms glutamatergic synapses with L7 motor neurons.
source: To examine synapse formation, we cultured a single bifurcated Aplysia SN with a target (L7) MN, with which it formed glutamatergic synapses, and a non-target (L11) MN, with which it fasciculated but did not form chemical synapses (Glanzman et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system with a citation to prior work.

claim: A bifurcated Aplysia sensory neuron fasciculates with but does not form chemical synapses with L11 motor neurons.
source: To examine synapse formation, we cultured a single bifurcated Aplysia SN with a target (L7) MN, with which it formed glutamatergic synapses, and a non-target (L11) MN, with which it fasciculated but did not form chemical synapses (Glanzman et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system with a citation to prior work.

claim: 18S rRNA concentration did not differ significantly between SN branches contacting L7 target MN and branches contacting L11 non-target MN.
source: Quantification of 18S (Figure 1B,C) and 28S (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) RNA in the proximal SN branches did not reveal any significant difference in concentration in the branch contacting the L7 target MN and the branch contacting the L11 non-target MN.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: 28S rRNA concentration did not differ significantly between SN branches contacting L7 target MN and branches contacting L11 non-target MN.
source: Quantification of 18S (Figure 1B,C) and 28S (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) RNA in the proximal SN branches did not reveal any significant difference in concentration in the branch contacting the L7 target MN and the branch contacting the L11 non-target MN.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: S6-dendra2 ribosomal protein targeted equally to distal SN branches contacting target or non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 1E,F, S6-dendra2 targeted equally to distal SN branches contacting target or non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Ribosomes are delivered throughout the SN and are not targeted specifically from the soma to branches receiving synaptogenic signals.
source: Together, these data indicate that ribosomes are delivered throughout the SN and are not targeted specifically from the soma to branches receiving synaptogenic signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rRNA FISH and S6-dendra2 data.

claim: Sensorin mRNA localizes to distal sensory neurites.
source: As a candidate localized mRNA, we first examined the transcript encoding the SN-specific neuropeptide sensorin, which not only localizes to distal sensory neurites but also concentrates at synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of sensorin mRNA.

claim: Sensorin mRNA concentrates at synapses.
source: As a candidate localized mRNA, we first examined the transcript encoding the SN-specific neuropeptide sensorin, which not only localizes to distal sensory neurites but also concentrates at synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of sensorin mRNA.

claim: The neuritic and synaptic localization of sensorin mRNA are mediated by distinct signals.
source: We have previously shown that the neuritic and synaptic localization of sensorin mRNA are mediated by distinct signals (Meer et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2009) and that sensorin mRNA undergoes localized translation at synapses during 5HT-mediated LTF (Wang et al. 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Sensorin mRNA undergoes localized translation at synapses during 5HT-mediated LTF.
source: We have previously shown that the neuritic and synaptic localization of sensorin mRNA are mediated by distinct signals (Meer et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2009) and that sensorin mRNA undergoes localized translation at synapses during 5HT-mediated LTF (Wang et al. 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Sensorin mRNA localized equally to both proximal and distal branches of bifurcated sensory neurons contacting L7 or L11 MNs.
source: FISH for sensorin mRNA in 3DIV cultures revealed that the sensorin transcript localized equally to both proximal (Figure 2D) and distal (Figure 2B,C) branches of bifurcated sensory neurons contacting L7 or L11 MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2B,C,D.

claim: The pattern of sensorin mRNA distribution was distinct in distal branches, with diffuse distribution in branches contacting non-target MNs and punctate concentrations at SN synapses onto target MNs.
source: The pattern of sensorin mRNA in distal branches was distinct, with diffuse distribution of sensorin mRNA in branches contacting non-target MNs and punctate concentrations of sensorin RNA at SN synapses onto target MNs (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A for quantification of coefficient of variation).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and coefficient of variation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The same amount of sensorin RNA was present in both SN branches contacting target and non-target MNs.
source: However, the same amount of RNA was present in both SN branches.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the FISH experiments.

claim: There is no directed targeting of sensorin mRNA from soma to branches receiving synaptogenic signals.
source: These findings are consistent with a lack of directed targeting of sensorin mRNA from soma to branches receiving synaptogenic signals, although there is local redistribution of sensorin mRNA within the neuronal process at synaptic sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equal distribution of sensorin mRNA in both branches.

claim: There is local redistribution of sensorin mRNA within the neuronal process at synaptic sites.
source: These findings are consistent with a lack of directed targeting of sensorin mRNA from soma to branches receiving synaptogenic signals, although there is local redistribution of sensorin mRNA within the neuronal process at synaptic sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the punctate pattern of sensorin mRNA at synapses.

claim: β-thymosin mRNA was distributed equally well in SN branches contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, β-thymosin mRNA was distributed equally well in SN branches contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: EF1α was expressed at very low levels in unstimulated neurons.
source: EF1α was expressed at very low levels in unstimulated neurons and was distributed equally well between L7 target and L11 non-target branches (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: EF1α was distributed equally well between L7 target and L11 non-target branches in unstimulated neurons.
source: EF1α was expressed at very low levels in unstimulated neurons and was distributed equally well between L7 target and L11 non-target branches (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: EF1α expression was significantly induced following five spaced bath applications of 5HT.
source: Its expression was significantly induced following five spaced bath applications of (5HT), as previously described (Giustetto et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and by FISH data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Equal amounts of 5HT-induced EF1α were delivered to SN branches contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 3C,D, we found that equal amounts of 5HT-induced EF1α were delivered to SN branches contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Activity-induced transcripts are not delivered preferentially from the nucleus towards a synaptic target.
source: These results indicate that activity-induced transcripts are not delivered preferentially from the nucleus towards a synaptic target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equal distribution of EF1α mRNA after 5HT stimulation.

claim: Local stimulation with 5x5HT induced expression of EF1α in the soma.
source: As shown in Figure 3, FISH for EF1α revealed that local stimulation with 5x5HT-induced expression of EF1α, as evidenced in increase in EF1α signal in the soma (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Following local stimulation, the stimulated EF1α transcript was delivered equally well to both stimulated and unstimulated branches.
source: Strikingly, the stimulated transcript was delivered equally well to both branches (Figure 3F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3F,H.

claim: Even following local stimulation, transcriptionally induced mRNAs are delivered throughout the neuronal arbor, to stimulated- and unstimulated-branches.
source: These studies reveal that even following local stimulation, transcriptionally induced mRNAs are delivered throughout the neuronal arbor, to stimulated- and unstimulated-branches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EF1α FISH data after local stimulation.

claim: ApStaufen-dendra2 was transported equally well to branches contacting target and non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 4, we found that ApStaufen-dendra2 was transported equally well to branches contacting target and non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Local stimulation with 5X5HT increased the number of ApStaufen-dendra2 puncta in the SN processes.
source: While local stimulation with 5X5HT increased the number of ApStaufen-dendra2 puncta in the SN processes (suggesting that local stimulation promotes the transport of RNAs out of the soma into the process), the increase was equivalent in stimulated- and unstimulated-SN branches.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in ApStaufen-dendra2 puncta following local stimulation was equivalent in stimulated- and unstimulated-SN branches.
source: While local stimulation with 5X5HT increased the number of ApStaufen-dendra2 puncta in the SN processes (suggesting that local stimulation promotes the transport of RNAs out of the soma into the process), the increase was equivalent in stimulated- and unstimulated-SN branches.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosomes, mRNAs, and RNA binding proteins are transported throughout the neuron, without any preferential targeting from the soma to branches receiving synaptic signals.
source: Together, our experiments using FISH to analyze rRNAs and sensorin and EF1α mRNAs, and overexpression to analyze S6 ribosomal protein and Staufen, argue that ribosomes, mRNAs, and RNA binding proteins are transported throughout the neuron, without any preferential targeting from the soma to branches receiving synaptic signals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Local translation is spatially restricted to stimulated synapses during synapse-specific long-term facilitation (LTF) of SN-MN synapses.
source: We have previously reported that local translation is spatially restricted to stimulated synapses during synapse-specific long-term facilitation (LTF) of SN-MN synapses (Wang et al 2009); here, we asked whether local translation is also spatially restricted during synapse formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Sensorin protein was present at much higher concentrations in SN branches contacting target MNs than in branches contacting non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 5B,C, sensorin protein was present at much higher concentrations in SN branches contacting target MNs than in branches contacting non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Sensorin expression is spatially regulated at the level of translational regulation rather than mRNA targeting.
source: These data are consistent with sensorin expression being spatially regulated at the level of translational regulation rather than mRNA targeting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equal mRNA distribution but differential protein concentration.

claim: Phosphorylated eIF4E concentration was significantly greater in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs.
source: Group data in (C) reveal that phospho-eIF4E, phospho-4EBP, and sensorin protein concentrations are significantly greater in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Phosphorylated 4EBP concentration was significantly greater in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs.
source: Group data in (C) reveal that phospho-eIF4E, phospho-4EBP, and sensorin protein concentrations are significantly greater in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Total eIF4E protein was distributed equally well in neurites contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, total eIF4E and total 4EBP protein were distributed equally well in neurites contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total 4EBP protein was distributed equally well in neurites contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, total eIF4E and total 4EBP protein were distributed equally well in neurites contacting L7 target and L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Translational machinery is distributed throughout the neuron but is preferentially activated at sites receiving a synaptogenic signal.
source: These findings indicate that translational machinery is distributed throughout the neuron but is preferentially activated at sites receiving a synaptogenic signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equal distribution of total translation factors but enriched phosphorylated forms at synapses.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF4E and 4EBP activates global translation.
source: Since phosphorylation of eIF4E and 4EBP activates global translation, our results indicate that translational regulation, rather than mRNA targeting, controls the locally regulated synaptic proteome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about translation regulation.

claim: Translational regulation, rather than mRNA targeting, controls the locally regulated synaptic proteome.
source: Since phosphorylation of eIF4E and 4EBP activates global translation, our results indicate that translational regulation, rather than mRNA targeting, controls the locally regulated synaptic proteome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential activation of translation factors at synapses.

claim: There was significantly more translation in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs, as measured by a sensorin-dendra2 translational reporter.
source: Group data (G) show that there is significantly more translation, measured as ΔF/F, in neurites contacting L7 target MNs than in neurites contacting L11 non-target MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data with a translational reporter shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Sensorin mRNA is preferentially translated at sites of synaptic contact.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that although sensorin mRNA is delivered throughout the SN, it is preferentially translated at sites of synaptic contact.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equal mRNA distribution but differential translation measured by the reporter.

claim: There was significantly more protein synthesis in SN varicosities contacting the synaptic L7 target MN than in SN contacts with the non-target L11 MN, as measured by ribopuromycylation.
source: As shown in Figure 6, these experiments revealed significantly more protein synthesis in SN varicosities contacting the synaptic L7 target MN than in SN contacts with the non-target L11 MN.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribopuromycylation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Synapse formation does not alter RNA targeting within the neuron but rather spatially regulates translation.
source: These results provide further evidence that synapse formation does not alter RNA targeting within the neuron but rather spatially regulates translation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ribopuromycylation data showing differential translation at synapses.

claim: Serotonin-regulated translation occurs specifically at stimulated synapses.
source: Our previous study using translational reporters to visualize local translation of sensorin mRNA during LTF of Aplysia SN-MN synapses (Wang et al., 2009) revealed that serotonin-regulated translation specifically at stimulated synapses and that this regulation required a calcium-dependent trans-synaptic signal from the MN to the SN (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Serotonin-regulated translation requires a calcium-dependent trans-synaptic signal from the MN to the SN.
source: Our previous study using translational reporters to visualize local translation of sensorin mRNA during LTF of Aplysia SN-MN synapses (Wang et al., 2009) revealed that serotonin-regulated translation specifically at stimulated synapses and that this regulation required a calcium-dependent trans-synaptic signal from the MN to the SN (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Sensorin protein was enriched at synaptic sites as compared to non-synaptic sites.
source: Our current finding that sensorin protein was enriched at synaptic sites as compared to non-synaptic sites (Figure 5B,C) is also consistent with a role for a synaptically localized translational regulation mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Netrin-1 is a chemotropic factor known to induce synaptogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Netrin-1 is a chemotropic factor known to induce synaptogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans (Colón-Ramos et al., 2007) and to stimulate translation in growth cones during axon guidance (Campbell and Holt, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Netrin-1 stimulates translation in growth cones during axon guidance.
source: Netrin-1 is a chemotropic factor known to induce synaptogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans (Colón-Ramos et al., 2007) and to stimulate translation in growth cones during axon guidance (Campbell and Holt, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Components of the translational machinery, including ribosomal subunits and translation factors, are tethered at the plasma membrane in neuronal dendrites by binding to the cytoplasmic tail of the netrin receptor DCC.
source: Flanagan and colleagues have reported that components of the translational machinery, including ribosomal subunits and translation factors, are tethered at the plasma membrane in neuronal dendrites by binding to the cytoplasmic tail of the netrin receptor Deleted in Colorectal Cancer (DCC), (Tcherkezian et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Netrin-1 binding triggers the release of bound translational components and promotes localized, netrin-1-dependent protein synthesis.
source: Netrin-1 binding was shown to trigger the release of bound translational components and to thereby promote localized, netrin-1- dependent protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Tcherkezian et al., 2010).

claim: Bath application of netrin-1 (250 ng/ml) for 24 hr increased sensorin immunoreactivity in SN branches contacting the L11 non-target MN.
source: As shown in Figure 7A,C, bath application of netrin-1 (250 ng/ml) for 24 hr increased sensorin immunoreactivity in SN branches contacting the L11 non-target MN, such that there was no longer any branch-specificity of sensorin protein concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: Bath application of netrin-1 eliminated the branch-specificity of sensorin protein concentration.
source: As shown in Figure 7A,C, bath application of netrin-1 (250 ng/ml) for 24 hr increased sensorin immunoreactivity in SN branches contacting the L11 non-target MN, such that there was no longer any branch-specificity of sensorin protein concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: Incubation with netrin-1 significantly increased sensorin immunoreactivity in SNs paired with target MNs.
source: As shown in Figure 7D,E, incubation with netrin-1 significantly increased sensorin immunoreactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Netrin-1 increased sensorin concentration equally well in branches contacting both L7 and L11 MNs in cultures in which the SN soma was removed.
source: These experiments revealed that netrin-1 increased sensorin concentration equally well in branches contacting both L7 and L11 MNs, consistent with local stimulation of translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Netrin-1 increased peIF4E immunoreactivity in SN-LFS cultures in which the SN soma had been removed.
source: Netrin-1 also increased peIF4E immunoreactivity in SN-LFS cultures in which the SN soma had been removed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The netrin-1-induced increase in sensorin immunoreactivity in intact SN-LFS cocultures was similar to that observed with five spaced applications of serotonin (5HT).
source: The netrin-1-induced increase in sensorin immunoreactivity in intact SN-LFS cocultures was similar to that observed with five spaced applications of serotonin (5HT), which produces LTF of SN-MN synapses and which has been shown to promote sensorin translation (Figure 7E) (Hu et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7E and citations to prior work.

claim: Netrin-1-induced translation in intact or soma-lacking SNs was blocked by pre-incubation with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin.
source: Moreover, netrin-1-induced translation in intact or soma-lacking SNs was blocked by pre-incubation with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin (10 μM for 24 hr), indicating that the increased immunoreactivity did indeed result from increased translation (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Incubation of SN-L11 cocultures or L7-SN-L11 cocultures with netrin-1 did not result in the formation of synapses.
source: However, incubation of SN-L11 cocultures or L7-SN-L11 cocultures with netrin-1 did not result in the formation of synapse as shown by the absence of an excitatory post-synaptic potential (EPSP) in the L11 MN after SN stimulation (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements (data not shown).

claim: Incubation with netrin-1 significantly increased EPSP amplitude between SN and LFS target MNs.
source: We did find, however, that incubation with netrin-1 significantly increased EPSP amplitude between SN and LFS target MNs (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: The increase in EPSP amplitude induced by netrin-1 was similar to that seen during LTF induced by five spaced applications of 5HT.
source: The increase in EPSP amplitude was similar to that seen during LTF induced by five spaced applications of 5HT (data not shown).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior observations (data not shown).

claim: Netrin-1 significantly increased the number of SN synaptic varicosities in SN-LFS MN cultures.
source: We thus measured the effect of netrin-1 on varicosity numbers, and, as shown in Figure 7H, found that it significantly increased the number of SN synaptic varicosities in SN-LFS MN cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The local translation induced by netrin-1 increases synaptic strength and synapse number.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the local translation induced by netrin-1 increases synaptic strength and synapse number.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the netrin-1 effects on EPSP amplitude and varicosity number.

claim: A 24 hr incubation of isolated SNs with netrin-1 triggered a significant increase in sensorin immunoreactivity.
source: We first showed that a 24 hr incubation of isolated SNs with netrin-1 triggered a significant increase in sensorin immunoreactivity, but that incubation of isolated SNs with anti-DCC (in the absence of netrin-1) did not change sensorin immunoreactivity (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Incubation of isolated SNs with anti-DCC (in the absence of netrin-1) did not change sensorin immunoreactivity.
source: We first showed that a 24 hr incubation of isolated SNs with netrin-1 triggered a significant increase in sensorin immunoreactivity, but that incubation of isolated SNs with anti-DCC (in the absence of netrin-1) did not change sensorin immunoreactivity (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased basal sensorin immunoreactivity in SN-MN cocultures.
source: While anti-DCC antibodies had no effect on the basal concentration of sensorin in isolated SNs, they significantly decreased basal sensorin immunoreactivity in SN-MN cocultures (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Netrin-1 is endogenously released from the post-synaptic MN and binds to DCC on the SN to promote pre-synaptic translation of sensorin.
source: Taken together, these findings are consistent with netrin-1 being endogenously released from the post-synaptic MN and binding to DCC on the SN to promote pre-synaptic translation of sensorin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of anti-DCC antibodies in isolated SNs versus SN-MN cocultures.

claim: SN-LFS MN pairs incubated with anti-DCC antibodies showed significantly smaller EPSP amplitudes than control cultures.
source: SN-LFS MN pairs incubated with anti-DCC antibodies also showed significantly smaller EPSP amplitudes than do control cultures (E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased sensorin and peIF4E immunoreactivity in SN-MN cocultures during synapse formation.
source: Group data (D) show that anti-DCC significantly decreases sensorin and peIF4E immunoreactivity, consistent with netrin being released from the MN to drive translation in the SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased sensorin and peIF4E immunoreactivity in mature, established SN-LFS MN synapses.
source: Group data show that anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased sensorin and peIF4E immunoreactivity (G) and EPSP amplitude between SN-LFS MNs (H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8G,H.

claim: Anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased EPSP amplitude in mature, established SN-LFS MN synapses.
source: Group data show that anti-DCC antibodies significantly decreased sensorin and peIF4E immunoreactivity (G) and EPSP amplitude between SN-LFS MNs (H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Netrin-1/DCC signaling contributes to synapse stability/maintenance.
source: As shown in Figure 8E, this also triggered a significant decrease in EPSP amplitude (Figure 8H) and sensorin immunoreactivity (Figure 8D), consistent with netrin-1/DCC signaling contributing to synapse stability/maintenance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of anti-DCC antibodies on established synapses.

claim: Aplysia Netrin-1 (ApNetrin-1) is 47% identical and 60% conserved with human Netrin-1.
source: Aplysia Netrin-1 (ApNetrin-1, accession #KM218335) was 47% identical and 60% conserved with human Netrin-1, and Aplysia DCC (ApDCC, accession # KM218336) was 31% identical and 47% conserved with human DCC.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of cloned Aplysia genes.

claim: Aplysia DCC (ApDCC) is 31% identical and 47% conserved with human DCC.
source: Aplysia Netrin-1 (ApNetrin-1, accession #KM218335) was 47% identical and 60% conserved with human Netrin-1, and Aplysia DCC (ApDCC, accession # KM218336) was 31% identical and 47% conserved with human DCC.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of cloned Aplysia genes.

claim: Overexpression of dendra2-tagged ApNetrin-1 in MNs significantly increased the concentration of sensorin protein in the SN.
source: Overexpression of ApNetrin-1 in the MN significantly increased the concentration of sensorin protein in the SN as measured by immunocytochemistry (Figure 9B,C), consistent with a netrin-1-dependent stimulation of translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 9B,C.

claim: ApNetrin-1 significantly increased synaptic strength between SN and MN.
source: Measurement of EPSP amplitude before and 24 hr after overexpression of dendra2-ApNetrin-1, or overexpression of dendra2 as a negative control, revealed that ApNetrin-1 significantly increased synaptic strength between SN and MN (Figure 9E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Despite being expressed in the MN, the majority of the ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal was found outside of the MN, decorating the processes of the SN.
source: As shown in Figure 10, despite being expressed in the MN, the majority of the ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal was found outside of the MN, decorating the processes of the SN, suggesting that ApNetrin-1 was released from the MN and bound to the SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10.

claim: ApNetrin-1 was released from the MN and bound to the SN.
source: As shown in Figure 10, despite being expressed in the MN, the majority of the ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal was found outside of the MN, decorating the processes of the SN, suggesting that ApNetrin-1 was released from the MN and bound to the SN.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of ApNetrin-1 signal on SN processes.

claim: Incubation with anti-DCC antibodies dramatically decreased the binding of ApNetrin-1 to the SN.
source: As shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1, incubation with anti-DCC antibodies dramatically decreased the binding of ApNetrin-1 to the SN, as assayed using Pearson's Correlation to monitor the colocalization of green ApNetrin-1-dendra2 and red DCC-mCherry.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and colocalization analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: When calcium was chelated in the MN by microinjection of BAPTA, green ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal was sequestered in the MN and did not colocalize with the SN.
source: As shown in Figure 10B,D, when calcium was chelated in the MN, green ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal was sequestered in the MN and did not colocalize with the SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10B,D.

claim: In the absence of BAPTA, the green ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal decorated the processes of the SN.
source: In contrast, in the absence of BAPTA, the green ApNetrin-1-dendra2 signal decorated the processes of the SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10B,D.

claim: ApNetrin-1 release from the MN is calcium-dependent.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with calcium-dependent release of ApNetrin-1 from the MN and binding to the SN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BAPTA experiments showing calcium-dependent release.

claim: The spatial regulation of gene expression in Aplysia sensory-motor neurons is mediated primarily at the level of translation rather than at the level of RNA targeting from the nucleus.
source: These results indicate that the spatial regulation of gene expression in Aplysia sensory-motor neurons is mediated primarily at the level of translation rather than at the level of RNA targeting from the nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the RNA localization and translation experiments.

claim: Netrin-1/DCC signaling promotes translation at synapses.
source: These results, together with our previous study (Wang et al., 2009) suggested the existence of a trans-synaptic signal that promotes translation of localized mRNAs. In investigating the nature of such a trans-synaptic signal, we uncovered a role for netrin-1/DCC signaling in local translation at synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the netrin-1 and anti-DCC experiments.

claim: Neurons deliver transcripts and translational machinery throughout the neuron, but a synaptically restricted netrin-1-dependent signal triggers localized translation at synapses.
source: Our findings are thus consistent with neurons delivering transcripts and translational machinery throughout the neuron, but with a synaptically restricted netrin-1-dependent signal triggering localized translation at synapses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating all the findings.

claim: Over 70% of mRNAs in Drosophila embryos are expressed in highly specific subcellular patterns.
source: For example, high throughput FISH analyses of over 3000 transcripts in Drosophila embryos indicated that over 70% of mRNAs were expressed in an array of highly specific subcellular patterns (Lécuyer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hundreds of mRNAs localize to neurites of Aplysia SNs.
source: We have previously identified hundreds of mRNAs in the neurites of Aplysia SNs (Moccia et al., 2003), and studies of localized mRNAs in mammalian hippocampal neurons have indicated that hundreds (Eberwine et al., 2002; Poon et al., 2006) to thousands of transcripts (Cajigas et al., 2012) localize to dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hundreds to thousands of transcripts localize to dendrites in mammalian hippocampal neurons.
source: We have previously identified hundreds of mRNAs in the neurites of Aplysia SNs (Moccia et al., 2003), and studies of localized mRNAs in mammalian hippocampal neurons have indicated that hundreds (Eberwine et al., 2002; Poon et al., 2006) to thousands of transcripts (Cajigas et al., 2012) localize to dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Arc mRNA localizes to stimulated synapses in mammalian dentate granule neurons.
source: While some studies have indicated that a handful of these mRNAs localize to specific subcellular loci within the neuronal process, including sensorin mRNA, which localizes to synapses in Aplysia SNs (Lyles et al., 2006), and arc mRNA, which localizes to stimulated synapses in mammalian dentate granule neurons (Steward et al., 1998), whether or not mRNAs undergo directed targeting from the soma to specific synapses, and whether or not RNA localization defines the fate of specific neuronal compartments, remains an open question.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The local proteome was regulated at the level of translation rather than by stimulus-induced mRNA targeting from the nucleus.
source: Using this preparation, we find that the local proteome was regulated at the level of translation rather than by stimulus-induced mRNA targeting from the nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments in the Aplysia system.

claim: Transcripts, ribosomes, and translational machinery were delivered throughout the neuron, but translation was selectively activated in response to local stimuli such as synapse formation.
source: Thus, transcripts, ribosomes, and translational machinery were delivered throughout the neuron, but translation was selectively activated in response to local stimuli such as synapse formation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Transcripts that are induced by stimuli are delivered throughout the neuron, with their local distribution and translation being regulated by localized cues.
source: Thus, transcripts that are induced by stimuli are delivered throughout the neuron, with their local distribution and translation being regulated by localized cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EF1α experiments showing equal distribution of induced transcripts.

claim: Netrin-1 binding to DCC may promote translation by releasing translational machinery from binding DCC cytoplasmic domains within the pre-synaptic terminal.
source: Netrin-1 binding to DCC may promote translation by releasing translational machinery from binding DCC cytoplasmic domains within the pre-synaptic terminal, as proposed by Flanagan et al. (2010).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on prior work.

claim: Netrin-1-induced translation may be downstream of PI3 kinase and/or MAPK pathways, both of which are activated by netrin-1 binding to DCC.
source: Alternatively, netrin-1-induced translation may be downstream of PI3 kinase and/or MAPK pathways, both of which are activated by netrin-1 binding to DCC (Li et al., 2004; Round and Stein, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on prior work showing pathway activation.

claim: Serotonin-induced translation of sensorin in SNs required a calcium-dependent retrograde signal from the MN.
source: We previously reported that serotonin-induced translation of sensorin in SNs required a calcium-dependent retrograde signal from the MN (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ApNetrin expressed in MN is released and binds to the SN in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: In the present study, we show that ApNetrin expressed in MN is released and binds to the SN in a calcium-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the BAPTA experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: Spontaneous release of glutamate from the pre-synaptic SN during synapse formation and/or during synaptic plasticity may be the source of calcium for netrin-1 release.
source: One possibility is that it results from spontaneous release of glutamate from the pre-synaptic SN during synapse formation and/or during synaptic plasticity (Eliot et al., (1994); Jin et al., (2012); Villareal et al., (2007)), although see also Sutton et al. (2006), which indicates that spontaneous release serves to suppress local translation in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citations to relevant prior work.

claim: Netrin-1/DCC signaling is one of multiple local cues and signaling pathways that regulate translation in neurons.
source: We suspect that netrin-1/DCC signaling is one of multiple local cues and signaling pathways that regulate translation in neurons and that translation is not regulated in a digital on/off manner, but rather in a graded manner.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Translation is not regulated in a digital on/off manner, but rather in a graded manner.
source: We suspect that netrin-1/DCC signaling is one of multiple local cues and signaling pathways that regulate translation in neurons and that translation is not regulated in a digital on/off manner, but rather in a graded manner.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to explain residual translation at non-synaptic sites.

claim: Synapse formation alters the localization of sensorin mRNA such that it concentrates at synapses.
source: Our previously published report that synapse formation alters the localization of sensorin mRNA such that it concentrates at synapses (Lyles et al., 2006; Meer et al., 2012), and that serotonin-regulated translation of a sensorin-based translational reporter was restricted to sites of synaptic contact, suggested that the activity-dependent synaptic localization of mRNA played a critical role in the regulation of its translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The precise subcellular localization of sensorin mRNA is secondary to the localization of the netrin-1 signal.
source: Our current finding that netrin-1 increases translation at synaptic and non-synaptic sites indicates that the precise subcellular localization of the mRNA is secondary to the localization of the netrin-1 signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the netrin-1 experiments showing translation at non-synaptic sites.

claim: Sensorin mRNA does not have to be in the synaptic milieu per se to be translated but rather has to localize to a site in which netrin-1/DCC signaling can occur.
source: Thus, sensorin mRNA does not have to be in the synaptic milieu per se to be translated but rather has to localize to a site in which netrin-1/DCC signaling can occur.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the netrin-1 findings.

claim: There was an increase in the concentration of sensorin mRNA in SN branches contacting target as compared to non-target MNs in more mature (5 DIV) cocultures.
source: We also note that we previously found that there was an increase in the concentration of sensorin mRNA in SN branches contacting target as compared to non-target MNs in more mature (5 DIV) cocultures (Lyles et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: While there is not directed targeting of sensorin mRNA from soma to process during synapse formation, there may be preferential stabilization, over time, of sensorin mRNA at sites of synaptic contact.
source: This suggests that while there is not directed targeting of sensorin mRNA from soma to process during synapse formation, there may be preferential stabilization, over time, of sensorin mRNA at sites of synaptic contact.
evidence: This is an interpretation reconciling the current findings with prior observations.

claim: Regulated RNA degradation functions to localize mRNAs and to limit translation within axons.
source: This finding is consistent with recent studies indicating that regulated RNA degradation functions to localize mRNAs and to limit translation within axons (Colak et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Netrin-1 was able to induce an equivalent increase in sensorin in SN neurites in the presence or absence of a SN soma.
source: Although one cannot directly compare the total concentration of sensorin in intact SN and isolated SN neurites, our data indicate that netrin-1 is able to induce an equivalent increase in SN neurites in the presence or absence of a SN soma.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Local translation contributes substantially to stimulus-induced changes in the local proteome.
source: This suggests that local translation contributes substantially to stimulus-induced changes in the local proteome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of netrin-1 effects with and without soma.

claim: A large number of transcripts, and not just the two mRNAs detected by FISH, localize throughout the neuronal arbor.
source: The fact that netrin-1 was able to stimulate global translation at non-synaptic sites as detected by phospho-eIF4E immunocytochemistry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) suggests that a large number of transcripts, and not just the two mRNAs we detected by FISH, localize throughout the neuronal arbor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the global translation marker data.

claim: Every type of RNA imaged was delivered from the soma throughout the neuronal arbor, whether during synapse formation or following local stimulation.
source: Moreover, we found that every type of RNA that we imaged was delivered from the soma throughout the neuronal arbor, whether during synapse formation or following local stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the RNA localization findings.

claim: Every measure of translation employed demonstrated localized translation at synapses and/or stimulated synapses.
source: In contrast, we found that every measure of translation that we employed demonstrated localized translation at synapses and/or stimulated synapses.
evidence: This is a summary of the translation findings.

claim: A signaling pathway involved in axon guidance also regulates synapse formation by spatially restricting neuronal gene expression.
source: Taken together, our findings show that a signaling pathway involved in axon guidance also regulates synapse formation by spatially restricting neuronal gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the role of netrin-1/DCC signaling.

claim: Stimuli trigger transcription of a population of mRNAs that are delivered throughout the neuron, but local cues independently regulate their translation.
source: Our findings further underscore an uncoupling of transcriptional and translational regulation in neurons, with stimuli triggering transcription of a population of mRNAs that are delivered throughout the neuron, but with local cues independently regulating their translation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating the findings on RNA distribution and localized translation.

claim: Decentralizing the control of gene expression to individual subcellular compartments enriches the adaptability and plasticity of the nervous system by enabling each compartment to change its proteome in response to local cues.
source: Decentralizing the control of gene expression to individual subcellular compartments in this manner enriches the adaptability and plasticity of the nervous system by enabling each compartment to change its proteome in response to local cues.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: This mechanism allows all the branches of a neuron to be in a state of readiness to respond to local stimuli by changing their local proteome and hence their synaptic structure and function.
source: This mechanism allows all the branches of a neuron to be in a state of readiness to respond to local stimuli by changing their local proteome and hence their synaptic structure and function.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion about the functional significance of the findings.
